evidenceAudit.scope: Adults (SDCPG adult pathway: above 14 years and over 50 kg). Not for children, pregnancy (immediate obstetric input) or haemodynamically unstable patients (ICU). Every number on this page was checked against SDCPG 2021 pp. 71–74, the 2024 international consensus or the 2009 ADA consensus. Clinical approval is pending.
findings: Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
SDCPG and the 2024 consensus differ on several thresholds; both are shown in the comparison table and a local protocol must choose one.

pathophysiology.summary: DKA is a state of cellular starvation and runaway catabolism caused by two failures at once: absolute or relative insulin deficiency and an excess of counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol and growth hormone).
keyMechanisms: Hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis: without insulin, tissues cannot take up glucose while glucagon drives hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Glucose spills into the urine and pulls water, sodium and potassium with it, causing profound dehydration.
Lipolysis and ketogenesis: fat is broken down to free fatty acids, which the liver oxidises to ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate and acetone).
Acidosis: ketoacids consume bicarbonate, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul breathing is the respiratory compensation.

Potassium paradox: acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium is often normal or high despite a total-body deficit of 3–6 mmol/kg. Insulin drives it back in, so check potassium before insulin.
Euglycaemic DKA: about 10% present with glucose below 11.1 mmol/L, most often with SGLT2 inhibitors, reduced intake, pregnancy or alcohol.
HHS is the other end of the spectrum: enough insulin to prevent ketosis but not hyperglycaemia, so dehydration and hyperosmolality dominate. One-third of crises are mixed DKA–HHS.

references.title: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report

symptoms: Onset: hours to a few days (HHS: days to weeks).
Volume depletion: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, weakness.

Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain in more than half. Abdominal pain correlates with the severity of acidosis and can mimic a surgical abdomen; if it does not settle as the acidosis corrects, look for a surgical cause.
Neurological: most patients are alert; drowsiness, stupor or coma occur in severe DKA and are more common in HHS.
physicalSigns: Dehydration: dry mucosa, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, shock in severe cases.
Respiratory: Kussmaul respiration (deep, rapid breathing) and a fruity acetone breath.
Signs of the trigger: chest, urine, skin or foot infection; features of myocardial infarction or an acute abdomen.
Record GCS: below 12 is an SDCPG severity marker.
precipitants: Infection: the most common trigger (urinary tract infection and pneumonia most often).
Insulin omission or insufficient insulin: the main cause of recurrent DKA.
SGLT2 inhibitors: can cause euglycaemic DKA.
Acute illness: myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis, surgery; also alcohol and drugs that affect carbohydrate metabolism.
redFlags: SDCPG markers for HDU/ICU: GCS below 12; pH below 7.1; ketones above 6 mmol/L; bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L; potassium below 3.3 or above 6.0 mmol/L; systolic BP below 90 mmHg; SpO2 below 92% on air; pulse above 100 or below 60; urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h or AKI
Potassium below 3.3 mmol/L (SDCPG) or below 3.5 mmol/L (consensus): hold insulin and replace potassium first
New headache, confusion or falling consciousness during treatment: suspect cerebral oedema; senior help and early brain imaging
Pregnancy, heart failure, dialysis or frail older adult: standard fluid volumes are unsafe

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Glucose at least 33.3 mmol/L, effective osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg, ketones below 3.0 mmol/L, pH at least 7.3 and bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L. Older patient, slower onset, confusion common.
Hyperosmolar and ketotic (ketones at least 3.0 mmol/L or pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L). Treat as DKA but lower osmolality slowly.
Intake below about 500 kcal/day; glucose usually not high and acidosis mild.
Heavy alcohol use with a recent binge, vomiting and starvation; glucose may be normal or low.
Pregnant, vomiting; mixed acid–base picture. Involve obstetrics immediately.

differentials.condition: Surgical abdomen, sepsis or MI as the cause
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pain that persists after acidosis corrects, focal abdominal signs, raised lipase with imaging evidence of pancreatitis, ischaemic ECG or raised troponin.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Glucose at least 11.1 mmol/L, OR known diabetes at any glucose
Blood β-hydroxybutyrate at least 3.0 mmol/L, OR urine ketones 2+ or more
pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L (consensus) — SDCPG uses below 15 mmol/L
Mild: pH 7.25–7.30 or HCO3 15–18, alert · Moderate: pH 7.0–7.25 or HCO3 10–15, alert/drowsy · Severe: pH below 7.0 or HCO3 below 10, ketones above 6, stupor/coma → ICU

ruleIn.expectedFinding: At least 11.1 mmol/L. Can be below 11.1 in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2 inhibitor, fasting, pregnancy).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Diagnostic criterion. During treatment: add dextrose when it falls to 13–14 mmol/L; below 4.0 mmol/L treat hypoglycaemia.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h until resolution
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At least 3.0 mmol/L is diagnostic; above 6.0 mmol/L is severe.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Best marker of diagnosis and resolution (below 0.6 mmol/L). Urine ketones measure acetoacetate, lag behind and can mislead; captopril and valproate cause false positives.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h until resolution
ruleIn.expectedFinding: pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L (SDCPG: below 15).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Grades severity, sets level of care and tracks resolution (pH at least 7.3 or bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L). Bicarbonate therapy only if pH below 7.0 (SDCPG: 6.9).
pros: Faster and less painful than arterial sampling, with lower complication risk
Venous pH and bicarbonate are what the consensus uses for diagnosis, monitoring and resolution
cons: Does not measure oxygenation; use pulse oximetry, or an arterial gas in shock, severe respiratory distress or a suspected mixed acid–base disorder

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Before insulin, 2 h after starting insulin, then every 4 h
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Often normal or high at presentation despite a total-body deficit; falls by 1–2 mmol/L with treatment.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Above 5.2 (SDCPG) / 5.0 (consensus): no added potassium. 3.3–5.2: add 40 mmol/L (SDCPG) or 20–30 mmol/L (consensus). Below 3.3 (SDCPG) / 3.5 (consensus): hold insulin and replace. Target 4–5 mmol/L.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Often low because glucose draws water out of cells (translocational, not true hyponatraemia).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Correct for glucose: add about 1.6 mmol/L of sodium for every 5.6 mmol/L of glucose above normal (SDCPG: add 3 per 10 mmol/L above 5.5). A rising sodium as glucose falls is expected and is not a reason for hypotonic fluid.
Supports ketoacidosis; useful where ketone testing is unavailable. Do not use it to judge resolution: large volumes of 0.9% saline cause a hyperchloraemic normal-gap acidosis.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h; daily after resolution
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised in up to half (pre-renal AKI).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Usually recovers with fluids. Oliguria or AKI is an SDCPG severity marker and makes potassium replacement riskier.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Above 300 mOsm/kg suggests a hyperosmolar component.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: If raised, lower osmolality by no more than 3–8 mOsm/kg/h and sodium by no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: WBC 10–15 × 10⁹/L is usual in DKA from stress hormones.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Do not assume infection from a modest rise. WBC above 25 × 10⁹/L suggests infection and needs a search.

references.title: Hyperglycemic crises in adult patients with diabetes (ADA consensus)

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Phosphate often normal at first, then falls with insulin.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Replace phosphate only if below 1.0 mmol/L with muscle weakness or respiratory or cardiac compromise.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Peaked T waves with high potassium; ischaemic changes if MI is the trigger.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Attach a cardiac monitor and repeat the ECG if potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L (SDCPG order sheet); potassium above 6.0 mmol/L is an SDCPG severity marker.

ruleOut.testName: Infection screen; lipase; pregnancy test; HbA1c
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Positive cultures or urinalysis; raised lipase; positive pregnancy test; high HbA1c.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Blood and urine cultures if infection is suspected. Lipase can rise in DKA without pancreatitis, so interpret with imaging. A high HbA1c means the insulin regimen should be changed before discharge.

references.title: Hyperglycemic crises in adult patients with diabetes (ADA consensus)

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Respiratory symptoms, hypoxia, or no obvious trigger
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Pneumonia is a leading trigger; listed on the SDCPG adult order sheet.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Altered consciousness out of proportion to the acidosis, focal signs, or deterioration during treatment
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Cerebral oedema (rare in adults, about 30% mortality) or a stroke as the trigger.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: The consensus advises a low threshold for brain imaging when mental status changes.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Abdominal pain that persists after the acidosis has started to correct
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Appendicitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis or another surgical cause.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: DKA pain should settle with treatment; persistent pain needs further evaluation.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess, confirm and decide level of care
actions: ABC, GCS, IV access, weight. Send glucose, ketones, VBG, U&E, FBC before treatment.
Confirm D + K + A. Grade severity. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors.
Severe DKA, any SDCPG marker, HHS or critical trigger → HDU/ICU. Mild–moderate and alert → ED or step-down with close nursing.
ICU; give isotonic saline until BP stabilises. The SDCPG order sheet does not apply.

branches.condition: Pregnant, under 14 years or 50 kg or less
actions: Use the obstetric or paediatric DKA pathway; do not use the adult order sheet.

clinicalManagement.title: Fluids first
actions: 0.9% NaCl 1 L over hour 1 (no potassium).
Then 1 L over the next 2 h (no potassium), then 1 L over the next 4 h with potassium, then 100–250 mL/h (SDCPG order sheet; adults over 50 kg, SBP at least 90).
Consensus alternative: 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid 500–1000 mL/h for 2–4 h; correct the deficit over 24–48 h.

branches.condition: Older, heart failure, dialysis or pregnant
actions: 250 mL boluses with frequent reassessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Potassium gate, then fixed-rate insulin
actions: Never start insulin before the potassium result.
Fixed-rate IV soluble insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h (50 units in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl). No bolus (SDCPG).
Continue the patient's usual long-acting basal insulin.
Recheck potassium 2 h after insulin starts, then every 4 h; keep it at 4–5 mmol/L.
No potassium; recheck in 2 h.
Add 40 mmol KCl per litre, maximum 10 mmol/h (SDCPG). Consensus: 20–30 mmol/L.
Hold insulin, cardiac monitor, ECG.
Replace potassium (SDCPG: 40 mmol in 500 mL over 4 h; consensus: 10 mmol/h); restart insulin when above threshold.

clinicalManagement.title: As glucose falls: add dextrose, keep insulin running
actions: Insulin clears ketones; never stop it because glucose is normal.
SDCPG: glucose below 13 mmol/L → 5% dextrose in 0.9% NaCl at 100–250 mL/h, keep insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/h; reduce to 0.05 only if glucose is below 6 mmol/L.
Consensus: glucose below 13.9 mmol/L → add 5–10% dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 unit/kg/h; aim for glucose about 11 mmol/L.
25 mL of 50% dextrose; recheck and review the infusion.
Start 5–10% dextrose with the saline from the outset so insulin can be given.

clinicalManagement.title: Only if indicated: bicarbonate, phosphate, VTE prophylaxis
actions: No routine bicarbonate: no benefit, and risk of hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.
No routine phosphate.
Prophylactic LMWH unless contraindicated (local VTE protocol).
Consensus: 100 mmol 8.4% sodium bicarbonate in 400 mL sterile water every 2 h until pH above 7.0. SDCPG: 50 mmol in 200 mL at 200 mL/h; hold if K below 3.3.

branches.condition: Phosphate below 1.0 mmol/L with weakness or cardiorespiratory compromise
actions: 20–30 mmol potassium phosphate in the fluids (check local availability; not found in the SFDA register).

clinicalManagement.title: Resolution and switch to subcutaneous insulin
actions: Resolved: ketones below 0.6 mmol/L AND pH at least 7.3 or bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L, and eating and drinking. Do not use urine ketones or the anion gap.
Give subcutaneous insulin BEFORE stopping the infusion: SDCPG overlaps the first rapid-acting dose by 1 h; consensus gives basal insulin 1–2 h before stopping.
Insulin-naive: total daily dose 0.5–0.6 unit/kg/day as basal-bolus (about 0.3 unit/kg/day if frail or kidney failure). Known diabetes: usual dose unless control was poor.

branches.condition: Low bicarbonate but ketones below 0.6 after lots of saline
actions: Likely hyperchloraemic acidosis, not persistent DKA; do not delay the switch for this alone.

medicationPlan.note: Adults over 50 kg. Doses as stated in SDCPG 2021 or the 2024 consensus; where they differ, both are shown. SFDA registration checked 11 Oct 2026.

regimens.dose: 1 L over 1 h; 1 L over 2 h; 1 L over 4 h; then 100–250 mL/h
adjustments: 250 mL boluses if older, heart failure, dialysis or pregnant

regimens.dose: 0.1 unit/kg/h fixed rate; 50 units in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl; no bolus
regimens.duration: Until resolved and SC insulin overlapped
adjustments: Reduce to 0.05 unit/kg/h: consensus at glucose below 13.9; SDCPG at glucose below 6
Bolus 0.1 unit/kg IV/IM only if IV access delayed (consensus)
K below 3.3: hold insulin; 40 mmol in 500 mL over 4 h (SDCPG) or 10 mmol/h (consensus)
SDCPG narrative allows up to 40 mmol/h but its order sheet caps at 10 mmol/h
monitoring: K at 2 h, then every 4 h

regimens.patientGroup: Glucose below 13 (SDCPG) / 13.9 (consensus); from the start in euglycaemic DKA

regimens.dose: 100 mmol in 400 mL sterile water (consensus) or 50 mmol in 200 mL at 200 mL/h (SDCPG)

guidelineComparison.title: Saudi SDCPG vs international consensus: where they differ

values: Only if IV access is delayed
When glucose below 13.9 mmol/L, to prevent hypoglycaemia
HCO3 at least 18 and/or pH at least 7.3, closed anion gap, eating
Ketones below 0.6 and pH at least 7.3 or HCO3 at least 18; anion gap not used

guidelineComparison.note: Pick one protocol locally and apply it consistently; do not mix thresholds in one patient. Keeping insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/h (SDCPG) gives more insulin and needs dextrose and close glucose checks; the consensus reduces the rate because hypoglycaemia occurs in 16–28% of treated DKA.

learningObjectives: Diagnose, grade and treat adult DKA in the emergency department.
keyPoints: D + K + A: all three needed.
Fluids → check potassium → insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h. Never reverse the order.
Treat the ketones, not the glucose: add dextrose, keep insulin running.
Always look for the trigger, most often infection or missed insulin.

Discharge only with sick-day rules, ketone testing, insulin supply and follow-up in 2–4 weeks. SDCPG: people with type 2 diabetes who had unexplained ketoacidosis in the 3 months before Ramadan should not fast.
pitfalls: Starting insulin before the potassium result.
Stopping or cutting insulin because glucose is normal while ketones are still high.
Missing euglycaemic DKA in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor.
Calling infection on a WBC of 12 (stress leucocytosis is expected).
Using urine ketones or the anion gap to call resolution.
Stopping IV insulin without overlapping SC insulin → rebound DKA.
Standard fluid volumes in the elderly, heart failure or dialysis.
